newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: SFE wheat up strongly on weather, world concerns.
newsitem.headline: SFE wheat up strongly on weather, world concerns.

text.p: Sydney Futures Exchange (SFE) wheat futures moved up sharply in heavier trading on Monday as Australian dry weather worsened and on world supply concerns.
Near-term contracts traded on the SFE floor at A$6.00-A$9.00 a tonne higher. A total of 35 contracts sold, the biggest volume in many weeks.
Nearby May 1997 rose A$7.00 to A$187.50 on the trade, while January 1998 rose A$9.00 to A$183.00.
Settlement prices also rose strongly across the board, with near-term contracts up by A$4.00-A$6.00, more distant contracts up by about A$8.00 and January 1988 up A$10.00 to A$184.00.
The possibility of trade sanctions against Iran dampening world wheat prices if Australia was forced to unload millions of tonnes of discount wheat was not enough to hold the market back.

Gary Booth of Ord Minnett Jardine Fleming Futures Ltd said every day conditions south of Sydney on Australia's eastern side were getting drier and drier. Demand for feed by the cattle industry was also growing.

"The Sydney market is finally reacting to domestic supply concerns, what could be the emergence of drought conditions, strong demand from the livestock industry, Australian Wheat Board (AWB) sales and very low carryover stocks," he said.
The threat of the U.S. big winter chill killing off large areas was another important market factor, he said.
A downward market correction was likely in the next few days in reaction to Monday's gains and to the Iran crisis, he said.
"I think that (Iran) will probably weigh on the U.S. market tonight and we may see prices retrace a little," he said.

But with soybeans at an eight and a half year high and ending stocks at 20 year lows in wheat and beans, weather anomalies or continued drought could produce real trouble, he said. All this was producing an erratic wheat market which could be headed for A$200.00, where resistance was likely, he said.
